title: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors
summary: Carbon monoxide comes from anything that burns fuel. You cannot see or smell it. Never run a generator, grill, camp stove or charcoal indoors or in a garage, never heat the house with an oven, keep battery CO alarms near where people sleep, and get everyone outside the moment one sounds.
doFirst: CO alarm sounding? Don’t look for the cause. Get everyone outside into fresh air now, then call 911 or the fire department if you can. Count heads. Don’t go back in until responders say you can (CPSC).
Someone has a headache, dizziness, sickness or confusion near something burning fuel? Get them and everyone else out into fresh air and open the Carbon monoxide poisoning protocol.
Never run a generator in the house, garage, basement, crawlspace, shed, porch or carport, even with doors and windows open (CDC, CPSC). See Generators.
Never burn charcoal, or use a grill, hibachi, fuel lantern or camp stove indoors, and never heat the house with a gas oven or range (CDC, CPSC).

blocks.p: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a deadly gas with no color and no smell. It comes from fuel that does not burn completely: coal, wood, charcoal, oil, kerosene, propane and natural gas, and from engines such as generators, cars, lawn mowers and power washers (CPSC). Furnaces, stoves, lanterns, fireplaces and gas ranges all make it (CDC).

You cannot see, smell or taste it, so people may not know they are breathing it (CPSC). Even with doors and windows open, a closed or partly closed space can trap it and let it build to deadly levels quickly (CPSC).

blocks.warn: Opening doors and windows does not make these safe inside: carbon monoxide still builds up to deadly levels (CDC, CPSC).

list: Generator: never inside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, or on a porch or in a carport, even with doors and windows open. Run it outside, more than 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents (CDC, CPSC). See Generators.
Charcoal: never burn it inside a home, garage, vehicle or tent (CPSC, CDC). Don’t cook on a charcoal grill in a garage, even with the garage door open (CPSC).

Fuel lanterns, hibachis and camp stoves: never use a charcoal grill, hibachi, lantern or portable camping stove inside a home, tent or camper (CDC, as in Water in winter and Shelter). For light, use flashlights or battery lanterns (CPSC says the same of candles: use flashlights or battery-operated candles instead).
Camp stoves and flameless chemical heaters: don’t use portable gas camp stoves or portable flameless chemical heaters indoors (CDC).
Oven, range or clothes dryer as a heater: never heat the house with a gas oven, range or dryer (CDC, CPSC). Never use an oven to heat your home (US Fire Administration).
Anything made for outdoor use: don’t use heat sources designed for outside use indoors; they make carbon monoxide (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Unvented stoves and fireplaces: don’t cook or burn anything on a stove or fireplace that isn’t vented (CDC).
A running vehicle: never run a car in an attached garage, even with the garage door open (CDC, CPSC).

A car stuck in snow: clear snow from the exhaust pipe, then run the engine and heater about 10 minutes each hour with one window slightly open. Everyone in the car stays awake while the engine runs; turn it off before anyone sleeps (National Weather Service, CDC, Red Cross; Carbon monoxide protocol). See Winter storms.

blocks.p: Fuel-burning heaters have their own rules: see Kerosene and propane heaters. For an unvented fuel-burning heater: “Turn it off when you go to sleep or leave the room, and never run it where anyone is sleeping (CPSC, US Fire Administration; Carbon monoxide protocol).”

list: Clear snow away from the outside vents of furnaces and other fuel-burning appliances (CPSC). Keep furnace and dryer vents clear of ice and snow, and check them during and after heavy snow (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).
A blocked furnace or gas dryer vent can let carbon monoxide build up inside. Newer furnaces may shut off completely, leaving the house without heat (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).
Make sure every gas heater is vented to the outside (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).
In normal times, have the heating system and any gas, oil or coal appliance serviced every year by a qualified technician, and have chimneys checked or cleaned every year (CDC).

blocks.warn: CDC: “Don’t cook or burn anything on a stove or fireplace that isn’t vented.” A vent-free gas fireplace is not vented, so the cautious rule is not to use it. If you run one anyway, do it only under every condition below.

blocks.p: A vent-free (unvented) gas fireplace, gas log set or wall heater has no chimney or flue. It runs on natural gas or propane from the house supply and may be wall-mounted, free-standing or set into a fireplace (New York State Department of Health). Unvented gas heaters release what they burn straight into your home (New York State Department of Health).

list: US Department of Energy: unvented combustion space heaters are not recommended for use inside your home.

New York State Department of Health: don’t use one as your main heat source, even during power failures. Running a generator outdoors for heat is a better option. The label New York requires on these heaters says it is a supplemental heat source and should not be the primary heat source.
Turn it off when you go to sleep or leave the room, and never run it where anyone is sleeping (CPSC, US Fire Administration; Carbon monoxide protocol).
Have working CO alarms in the house if you use one (US Department of Energy: install a carbon monoxide detector if you use a small space heater).
Have it installed by a professional, such as your gas supplier, and don’t buy one too big for the room (New York State Department of Health).
Turn it off when you go to bed or leave the room (US Fire Administration, NFPA).
Use alarms that run on batteries or have battery backup (CPSC, CDC). Plug-in and hard-wired alarms should have battery backup (CPSC).

Put one on every level of the house and outside each sleeping area (CPSC; New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services, citing NFPA). CDC: near every sleeping area. Interconnected alarms are best: when one sounds, they all sound (CPSC).
Keep them away from heating vents and from places furniture or curtains can cover them. Don’t put one in the kitchen or above a fuel-burning appliance (CPSC).
Buy alarms that meet UL 2034 (CPSC). New York law accepts alarms listed to UL 2034 or CSA 6.19 (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Test them every month (CPSC). The test button checks the circuit, not whether the sensor still works (CPSC). Check the batteries when the clocks change in spring and fall (CDC).
Replace each alarm at the age its maker gives, or every 5 years (CDC, CPSC).

blocks.p: New York law (Amanda’s Law, in force since February 22, 2010) requires CO alarms in one- and two-family homes, multifamily homes and rentals that have a fuel-burning appliance or system, or an attached garage (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).

blocks.warn: Never ignore a CO alarm. Don’t try to find where the gas is coming from (CPSC).

steps: Get everyone outside into fresh air right away (CPSC).
Call 911 or the fire department if you can (CPSC).
Count heads: make sure everyone is out (CPSC).

Don’t go back inside until emergency responders say you can (CPSC). If no responders can come, don’t go back in until the house has aired out and the cause is fixed (Carbon monoxide poisoning protocol).
If an appliance caused it, don’t use that appliance again until a trained person has serviced it (CPSC).
If the alarm sounds again within 24 hours of going back in, get out again and repeat these steps, and have a qualified technician check the house (CPSC).

blocks.p: The most common signs are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion (CDC). At first it feels like the flu without a fever (CPSC). People who are asleep or drunk can die before they notice anything (CDC).
If several people in the same house, room or vehicle feel this way near something burning fuel, think carbon monoxide. What to do is in the Emergency protocol.
